When I first started working with my master’s supervisor, every day was agony and I was constantly miserable. He was an odd man, often harsh, and, worst of all, academically he had almost nothing to offer.

Who’d have thought that when I went abroad, he would be the one who gave me the most support, “indulging” me by letting me set my project aside to apply to universities? He then introduced me to an eminent Chinese scientist in the UK, and it was thanks to that introduction that this big name wrote me a recommendation letter to the professor who later became my PhD supervisor.

So my feelings about my supervisor are complicated. Academically he gave me no help at all; my master’s project was entirely DIY. He often knocked me down, saying this or that was no good without ever giving a reason. Later, at the thank-you dinner that Chinese graduates throw for their teachers, he told me this was his method: teaching by discouragement. And yet, when it came to my going abroad, he was farsighted and backed me all the way.

So he mattered enormously to me! He gave me an early taste of the self-reliance a PhD demands, and then pushed me into one. It was painful at first, and I thought he was academically weak, but there is plenty besides academic ability that can have a profound influence on you. When all is said and done, my supervisor is a good man who truly has his students’ interests at heart, and that matters more than anything.
